summary:
Minnesota sets its own civil, health-care and criminal law within the federal framework of the United States; federal rules on passports, visas, entry screening and federal custody are fixed nationally and are not restated here. On the matters a trans visitor encounters at state level, Minnesota law runs in a protective direction.

Minnesota Session Law 2023 ch. 29 (HF 146) declares that gender-affirming health care as defined in the Act "is against the public policy of this state and must not be enforced or applied" in pending cases, and amends state provisions on warrants, arrests and extraditions that arise from other states' laws on gender-affirming health care. The House passed the bill 68-62 on 24 March 2023 after a late-night debate, and Governor Tim Walz signed it. It followed a March 2023 executive order directing the Minnesota Department of Health to summarise the scientific literature on the safety and effectiveness of gender-affirming care and confirming that providers could bill insurance for such care.

The shield reaches out-of-state process. Minnesota authorities may not enforce subpoenas, arrest warrants or extradition requests issued elsewhere over gender-affirming care that is legal in Minnesota, and may not comply with out-of-state court orders to remove children from parental custody for having obtained such care. Families travelling to Minnesota for treatment fall inside that protection.

Anti-discrimination law covers gender identity. Minnesota has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity since 1993 in employment, housing, public accommodations, insurance, goods and services, contracts, health benefits and hospital visitation rights, and in that year became the first state to outlaw discrimination based on sexual orientation in the same fields. A May 2023 omnibus community justice bill protected "gender identity" as a category separate from sexual orientation and repealed exemptions for nonpublic service organizations, effective immediately. The same act repealed residual statutory language stating that the state "does not condone homosexuality or bisexuality" and did not authorise its promotion in educational institutions.

Hate-crime law has provided additional penalties for offences committed because of gender identity since that category was added in 1993; sexual orientation was added in 1989. The trans panic defence was abolished by the omnibus justice reforms signed on 29 May 2024 and effective 1 August 2024, which passed the Senate 34-33.

Identity documents are relatively open at state level. Changing the gender marker on a Minnesota birth certificate does not require sex reassignment surgery: it requires a physician's letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a court order for gender change, plus a notarised Birth Certificate Application and a fee, and the previous certificate is kept confidential. Driver and Vehicle Services updates a driver's licence or state ID on individual request with no documentation required, and since October 2018 licences and state IDs offer M, F or X on request, with no documentation needed for intersex, non-binary and ambiguous-sex applicants. Birth certificates carry no X option.

Care coverage is written into state policy. State Medicaid covers transgender-related care, and Minnesota law bars health insurers from excluding transgender-specific coverage or discriminating against transgender patients. Gender-affirming services were protected by the March 2023 executive order and codified by the legislation signed in April 2023. Conversion therapy is banned for minors and vulnerable adults under a law signed by Governor Tim Walz on 26 April 2023 and effective 1 August 2023, following a July 2021 executive order and city bans beginning with Minneapolis in November 2019. Practitioners may not advertise LGBTQ identities as a mental disease, disorder or illness or promise to change sexual orientation or gender identity; violations are subject to discipline by health licensing boards, and insurers and health plans may not pay for conversion therapy.

Private consensual conduct between adults is not criminalised. Minn. Stat. 609.293, which punished voluntarily engaging in or submitting to sodomy by the anus or by or with the mouth with up to one year's imprisonment and a fine of up to $3,000, was declared unconstitutional on 15 May 2001 as applied to private, consensual, non-commercial acts of adults, on privacy grounds under the Minnesota Constitution, in an unappealed class action decided two years before Lawrence v. Texas. The prohibition had been carried since the 1849 territorial adoption of Wisconsin law and the 1851 code, was raised in 1909 to 20 years' imprisonment, was expanded in 1921 to include fellatio, and was reduced in 1967 to a misdemeanour punishable by up to one year in jail or a $1,000 fine; a 1973 repeal attempt failed 46-69 with 19 abstentions, and formal repeal came in May 2023 through the Omnibus Judiciary and Public Safety Bill signed by Governor Tim Walz.

Marriage is recognised for relationships read locally as same-sex. Same-sex marriage became legal in Minnesota on 1 August 2013, after House passage 75-59 on 9 May and Senate passage 37-30 on 13 May, signed by Governor Mark Dayton on 14 May, following the defeat of a constitutional ban by 51.5% to 47.5% on 6 November 2012. A trans visitor married to a partner of any birth-sex configuration is recognised on that footing.

Custody placement practice has been documented along birth-sex lines. CeCe McDonald, a transgender woman, pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter and was sentenced on 4 June 2012 to 41 months; her attorneys acknowledged there was "no way" she would be sent to a women's prison and "really no history of transgender people being placed according to their gender identity" in the state. The Minnesota Department of Corrections placed her in an adult male facility, Minnesota Correctional Facility - St. Cloud, after a state gender assessment concluded she would be held in a men's facility, and although she was later transferred to a second facility she remained quartered with men throughout her imprisonment. She was held in segregated custody while awaiting trial. In May 2012 a fellow inmate attacked her with a glass, causing a wound that required eleven stitches; the attacker pleaded guilty in April 2013 to third-degree assault and received six months' jail time plus probation. A petition filed during her imprisonment led the department to administer the correct hormone regimen.
tangentialFactors:
An independent legal-risk assessment published in July 2026 places Minnesota in its "Most Protective States" tier alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts and Maryland, the strongest category the assessment uses.

The state's protective posture sits alongside litigation over contested policies, including the challenge to its high school transgender athlete policy and the abolition of the trans panic defence, which passed the Senate by a single vote.
localsOnly:
Attorneys representing three school softball players have challenged Minnesota's high school transgender athlete policy in court.

Family formation law treats same-sex couples as adoptive and legal parents in practice. Single LGBTQ people may petition to adopt, and there is no specific prohibition on joint or stepchild petitions by same-sex couples; IVF is accessible, and a married non-genetic, non-gestational mother through donor insemination is recognised as a parent. Surrogacy is neither expressly prohibited nor expressly permitted, though courts have generally ruled for the couples involved. In re Guardianship of Kowalski, decided on 17 December 1991, awarded guardianship to a lesbian partner over the objections of the ward's parents. An August 2014 court settlement upheld the state's marriage and sexual-orientation employment discrimination laws against a hunting club that had refused to host a same-sex wedding.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources describe the text and passage of the 2023 shield law rather than decided cases applying it. Whether Minnesota courts have ruled on how it interacts with a specific out-of-state judgment, subpoena or custody order is unresolved on the available material.

Enforcement data for the state's hate-crime and non-discrimination provisions, including complaints, charges and outcomes involving gender identity, are not sourced here. Nor is any Minnesota-specific figure on violence against transgender residents or visitors; the only documented custody incident in the material is the 2012 placement case.

The outcome of the challenge to the high school transgender athlete policy is not recorded in the available sources, and no ruling on the scope of the conversion therapy ban is reported.
